author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: Eustathius interprets Psalm 15 to defend the full humanity of Christ's soul and the unity of his person.
argument: Eustathius argues that Jesus possessed a human soul as well as human flesh. He insists that the soul of Jesus is rational and of the same substance as human souls, just as his flesh is of the same substance as human flesh, having come from Mary. He then quotes or alludes to the formula 'God sent his Son, born of a woman' (cf. Galatians 4:4), stressing that it uses the singular, because the person of Christ is one. He denies that this means one nature, or that flesh and divinity share the same substance, but affirms one Lord Jesus Christ, known in the distinction of natures.

outline.move: Jesus had experience of both: he came to be in the region of human souls, and having come to exist apart from the flesh, lives and subsists.
The soul of Jesus is rational and of the same substance as human souls, just as his flesh is of the same substance as human flesh, having come from Mary.
God sent his Son born of a woman as one person; Eustathius denies saying 'one nature'—'far be it, let it not be'—or the same substance of flesh and divinity, but affirms one Lord Jesus Christ.

cast.name: Jesus Christ
cast.who: The one whose soul and flesh Eustathius discusses; the text does not explicitly call him 'incarnate Son of God'.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The mother from whom Christ's flesh came.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The Father who sent his Son.

voices.speaker: Eustathius of Antioch
voices.how_marked: The main voice of the commentary; the fragments are introduced as from his interpretation of Psalm 15.

key_terms.sense: The human soul of Jesus, which existed apart from the flesh and is rational.
The human flesh of Christ, taken from Mary.
Of the same substance or being; used of Christ's soul with human souls and his flesh with human flesh.
Rational, describing the soul of Jesus as a reasoning soul like human souls.
The single person of Christ, as opposed to a single nature.
Nature; Eustathius denies that Christ's person is one nature or that flesh and divinity share one nature.
Substance or essence; used to deny that flesh and divinity have the same substance.
Born of a woman, quoted from Galatians 4:4 to stress the singular person of the Son.

scripture: The author cites Psalm 15 according to the Septuagint numbering and quotes Galatians 4:4. Modern citations should use Psalm 15 (LXX) and Galatians 4:4.
uncertain: The exact date of the commentary within Eustathius's career.
Whether the fragments come from a continuous commentary on Psalm 15 or from separate exegetical notes.
The precise identity of the opponents Eustathius may be answering.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The text does call Jesus 'Son' (τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ) sent by God, born of a woman; the text does not explicitly call him 'incarnate Son of God'.
The names object should include 'Psalm 15' (ιεʹ ψαλμοῦ) as a referenced work, and possibly 'Galatians' or 'Paul' as the source of the quotation 'God sent his Son, born of a woman'.
